item.title: Election 2026: Tiburon council race pits five candidates over parks, housing, finances, traffic
item.description: Five candidates seek three seats on the Tiburon Town Council Nov. 3: incumbents Alice Fredericks and Jack Ryan, challengers Kathleen Defever, Chuck Hornbrook and Faris Jafar.
item.content:encoded:
Updated:12 minutes ago

Five candidates are competing for three seats on the Tiburon Town Council in the Nov. 3 election, with park amenities, financial transparency and housing at the center of the race.

Incumbent Councilmembers Alice Fredericks and Jack Ryan face challenges from Kathleen Defever, a member of the Planning Commission; Chuck Hornbrook, a member of the Parks, Open Space & Trails Commission; and Faris Jafar, who is seeking his first elected office.

At least one of the three challengers is guaranteed a seat because incumbent Mayor Jon Welner is not seeking reelection. The three winners will serve four-year terms until November 2030.

Election 2026: The Tiburon Town Council candidates at a glance

SEPT. 29 CANDIDATE FORUM:The Ark is hosting a Tiburon Town Council candidate forum moderated by the League of Women Voters of Marin County from 7 to 8:30 p.m. 29 at Town Hall. It is open to the public. Questions for the candidates can be submitted in advance toforum@thearknewspaper.comand can also be submitted at the event.

Election 2026:Read complete coverage atthearknewspaper.com/election2026

The Ark interviewed the five candidates in August about those issues, along with the future of the former sanitation ponds site near McKegney Green, the town’s use of Flock license-plate readers and strategies to reduce traffic.

The candidates will also discuss the town’s future at a forum hosted by The Ark and moderated by the League of Women Voters of Marin County from 7 to 8:30 p.m. Sept. 29 in the Town Hall council chambers at 1505 Tiburon Blvd.

Defever: Public’s priorities ‘are my priorities’

Kathleen Defever, 48, is seeking her first term on the council. She has served since 2018 on the Planning Commission, the town body that reviews the general plan, conditional-use permits, zoning and zoning text amendments.

This is her third run for the council. Defever lost to Ryan in the March 2020 special election and finished second to Noah Griffin in the November 2021 special election.

She is an attorney who has a solo practice in property- and disability-insurance litigation. Defever writes articles for law journals on consumer and insurance law and gives speeches to European lawyers about American insurance law.

Education:Bachelor’s and master’s degrees in psychology from California State University at Sacramento, a law degree from the University of San Francisco and a doctorate in behavioral medicine from the University of Miami in Coral Gables, Florida.

item.title: Election 2026: Four candidates vying for seats on Reed school board as bond measure looms
item.description: Four candidates seek three seats on the Reed Union School District board Nov. 3: incumbents Mike Ghaffary and Shelby Pasarell Tsai, challengers Krupa Antani and Lina Godfrey.
item.content:encoded:
The four candidates vying for three seats on the Reed Union School District board of trustees include two incumbents who say they want to build on what they’ve already accomplished in office and two newcomers who each say they would bring a different perspective to the board.

Current board members Mike Ghaffary and Shelby Pasarell Tsai and challengers Krupa Antani and Lina Godfrey are competing on the Nov. 3 ballot for the open spots on the five-member board.

The Reed Union School District candidates at a glance

Election 2026:Read complete coverage atthearknewspaper.com/election2026

Pasarell Tsai is seeking a second term after winning one of three seats in a four-way election in November 2022; she is the board president. Ghaffary was appointed to the board in February to fill the seat of longtime board member Sherry Wangenheim, who resigned in December 2025 with one year left on her term to move to London with her family.

The third seat belongs to Afsaneh Zolfaghari, who chose not to seek a third term.

The board race is one of two decisions facing Reed Union School District voters on the Nov. 3 ballot. Residents in the district, which includes Tiburon, Belvedere and east Corte Madera, will also decide whether to approve a $115 million bond measure that would fund upgrades at all three district campuses.

If the bond measure wins the 55% approval needed to pass, the winners of the board race will join their two other colleagues in overseeing how those funds are spent. The fate of the bond measure is just one issue facing the Reed district; other key initiatives for board candidates include continuing efforts to challenge all students academically, to balance the district budget without sacrificing student programs and to look critically at how technology is used in the classroom.

Ghaffary says financial background brings value to board

Ghaffary, 46, has lived in Tiburon for nearly seven years with his wife, Sophia, who serves on the board of the Belvedere-Tiburon Library Foundation. The couple has two children: Arthur, a seventh grader at Del Mar Middle School, and Aya, a fifth grader at Bel Aire Elementary School.

Ghaffary earned undergraduate degrees in computer science and political science from the University of Southern California and a master’s in business administration and a law degree from Harvard University. He is an inactive member of the California bar.

item.title: Tiburon Challenger tennis tournament levels up with a bigger purse and higher-ranked players
item.description: The Tiburon Challenger returns to the Tiburon Peninsula Club Sept. 13-20 with a $230,000 prize pot, more than double last year's, and a promotion to the ATP 125 level.
item.content:encoded:
The Tiburon Challenger tennis tournament returns to the Tiburon Peninsula Club Sept. 13 with a $230,000 prize pot and a promotion to the ATP Challenger Tour’s 125 level.

Now in its 18th year, the tournament will bring some of the world’s best rising male players to the Tiburon Peninsula. The prize money is more than double last year’s $100,000, and the event has moved up a tier from the tour’s 75 level.

The men will play over a week that ends with finals weekend Sept. 19 and 20. There will be three draws: 24 in singles qualifying, 32 in the singles main draw and 16 pairs in doubles.

New this year is The Village, a social hub on the club patio. People can buy food, drinks or clothing, play lawn games, sit on lounge seating or visit booths from vendors such as Brad Gilbert’s Tennis Nation. The Village will be open from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Sept. 13 and from 3 to 7 p.m. 14-18. Opening day doubles as Kid’s Day at The Village, following a free children’s tennis clinic that morning.

Finals weekend, the biggest draw, is sold out. But tennis fans can still catch the finale in another setting. The club will show the finals on a large LED screen on its patio Sept. 19 and 20 for a watch party open to members and guests. Finals weekend will also run live on the Tennis Channel, hosted by Mike Cation and Brad Gilbert.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister

item.title: Cypress Hollow Park redesign prompts calls for more changes
item.description: Parents told the Tiburon Parks, Open Space & Trails Commission on Aug. 24 that the proposed Cypress Hollow Park play structures don't look fun. The commission asked for changes.
item.content:encoded:
Neighbors and parents unhappy with the latest redesign of Cypress Hollow Park have prompted the parks commission to seek another round of changes, including different play structures and a ramp instead of stairs.

The Parks, Open Space & Trails Commission at its Aug. 24 meeting directed Santa Rosa-based Carlile Macy to take another pass on the 60%-complete designs it presented for the park. Those designs carried an estimated construction cost of $2.09 million. That direction came after several parents expressed disappointment with the play structures proposed, one of them saying the design “doesn’t look fun at all.”

Residents also criticized a proposed sidewalk around the park and the steps connecting the park’s upper and lower play areas, calling them a potential safety hazard.

Briana Morrison, associate principal and landscape architect with Carlile Macy, said the consultant would heed the feedback.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez

item.title: Tiburon parks commission weighs reservation system for new amenities
item.description: Tiburon has no simple way to reserve a picnic table or book a park for a party. The Parks, Open Space & Trails Commission voted 4-0 on Aug. 24 to form a reservations subcommittee.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon offers no simple way to reserve a picnic table or book a park for a party, and its parks commission wants a system in place before the town’s new parks open.

The Parks, Open Space & Trails Commission voted 4-0 at its Aug. 24 meeting to create a reservations subcommittee, appointing Vice Chair Nicole Voss and Commissioner Chuck Hornbrook to it. Commissioner Jonathan Kahn was absent.

Hornbrook raised the idea as the commission works through proposed amenities at the former sanitation ponds site near McKegney Green, including picnic tables under a shade awning.

“It would be a free-for-all,” Hornbrook said of trying to use the proposed picnic tables under existing rules. “It’d be me squatting that morning, protecting it from everyone else.”

Hornbrook also said he believed the community would prefer seeing proactive efforts from the commission “now, as opposed to like, ‘Oh shoot, we forgot about that.’”

item.title: Sanitary District No. 5 rejects grand jury push to consolidate
item.description: Sanitary District No. 5 of Marin County told the Marin civil grand jury Aug. 20 that its Belvedere and southern Tiburon sewer plant has no capacity to take on more customers.
item.content:encoded:
Belvedere and southern Tiburon’s sewer agency has told the Marin civil grand jury it sees no need to consolidate, saying its treatment plant has no room for more customers.

The grand jury, a panel of 19 county residents impaneled each year by the Superior Court to write government oversight reports, required responses from 34 governing bodies, 31 of them special districts. Its June 11 report, “Better Service at Lower Cost,” argued that Marin’s special districts should collaborate more aggressively and, where feasible, consolidate.

Sanitary District No. 5 of Marin County adopted its legally required response Aug. 20. The district said it has already consolidated, annexing Belvedere’s collection system in 2005 and Seafirth Estates in 2009. It also said the grand jury’s claims lack evidence that the district is inefficient.

Tony Rubio, the district manager, said in an interview the district is focused on its current customers and cannot take on more.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister

item.title: Peninsula residents lead the way in Run Tiburon 10K & 5K
item.description: Brad Geddes, 40, of Tiburon won the Run Tiburon 10K outright Aug. 30, covering the course in 39:46 to finish first among 319 entrants.
item.content:encoded:
Brad Geddes, 40, of Tiburon won the Run Tiburon 10K outright on Aug. 30, and local runners took four of the six podium spots among women in the 10K and 5K.

Geddes ran the 10K in 39 minutes, 46 seconds to finish first among 319 entrants and win the male 40-49 age group. He was ninth overall in the same race last year.

Kate Greer, 41, of Belvedere was the first woman across in the 10K, taking eighth overall in 40:51 and winning the female 40-49 division.

item.title: Strawberry Recreation District rejects grand jury’s term-limit recommendation
item.description: Strawberry Recreation District board voted unanimously Aug. 18 to reject a Marin civil grand jury recommendation that special districts limit members to two consecutive terms.
item.content:encoded:
Strawberry Recreation District board members can serve term after term without limit — Chair Peter Teese is in his fourth — and the board voted unanimously Aug. 18 to keep it that way. It rejected a Marin County civil grand jury recommendation that special districts cap members at two consecutive four-year terms by June 1, 2027.

Teese has served since December 2010, elected without opposition in 2014, 2018 and 2022. He is on the Nov. 3 ballot for a fifth term.

The other four members all joined since 2022. Marin County supervisors appointed Sohrab Saghezchi in December 2022, after no one filed for the seat. Christian Michael was appointed in April 2024 and won a four-year term that November. Sarah Waterfield won a two-year seat the same month. And the board appointed Doug Twillman in September 2025 to finish the term of Cale Nichols, who resigned after moving out of state.

The vote closes out the district’s response to “Better Service at Lower Cost,” the grand jury’s June 11 report on consolidating Marin’s special districts. The board rejected the rest of the report 4-0 on July 14, with Waterfield absent, arguing a fee-supported recreation district has little in common with the fire and sanitary agencies the grand jury studied, but set the term-limit recommendation aside for further review.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister

item.title: Everyday Encounters: A friendship that started in Tiburon and spans continents
item.description: Brian Suchodolski and Pep Gubau grew up together in Tiburon, played soccer at Redwood High and stayed close across 5,950 miles when Gubau moved back to Barcelona.
item.content:encoded:
Brian Suchodolski and Pep Gubau reminisce about a childhood friendship as they walk to Lola’s Taqueria from the corner of Tiburon Boulevard and Beach Road on Aug. 26. Both call the Mexican restaurant a favorite, and both say they’re fans of its burritos.

The two are more than lifelong friends. As Suchodolski puts it, Gubau is practically his brother. Obstacles to that friendship, including some 5,950 miles between two continents, are easy to overcome.

“When we see each other, it’s just like we haven’t been apart at all,” Suchodolski says.

The two 22-year-olds, who grew up in Tiburon, were separated when Gubau returned to Barcelona for his junior and senior years of high school. That, combined with the coronavirus pandemic, kept them from seeing each other for about 18 months, Gubau says.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: Pep Gubau (left) and Brian Suchodolski, both 22, stand at the corner of Tiburon Boulevard and Beach Road in Tiburon on Aug. 26 before walking to Lola’s Taqueria. The two grew up in Tiburon and became friends through soccer; Gubau moved from Barcelona at age 7 and returned there for his junior and senior years of high school. (Francisco Martinez / The Ark)

item.title: Robert Miller Chandler
item.description: Robert Miller Chandler died on August 12, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Robert Miller Chandler died on August 12, 2026, in San Francisco, California, shortly after returning from a bucket-list cruise through the Baltic region. His final words were, “I’m so happy to be home.”

Born during World War II on April 26, 1943, at St. Anne’s Hospital in Chicago, Illinois, Robert was the son of Spiros D. Charuhas, who immigrated to the United States from Greece through Ellis Island, and Lorraine Donham Charuhas, an Illinois native. He was raised in Chicago’s Lakeview neighborhood and attended Nettelhorst Elementary School, founded in 1892, and Lake View High School, founded in 1874. Both schools were recognized for academic excellence by the state of Illinois and the city of Chicago. Throughout his life, Robert cherished the memories of his childhood in Lakeview.

Robert graduated from Roosevelt University in Chicago in 1974 with a bachelor’s degree in marketing and a minor in finance. While there, he was a member of Pi Sigma Epsilon fraternity. Robert began his career owning and operating restaurants in Chicago with his father before changing paths in 1968, when he was recruited by FMC Corporation’s Power Transmission Division in Chicago as an account manager.

In 1973, Robert married Kathleen Allison MacArthur of Palatine, Illinois, whom he met at Roosevelt University. The couple moved to Tiburon, California, in 1974 and had two children: Steven, who became a lieutenant colonel and evaluator pilot in the U.S. Air Force and a pilot with United Airlines; and Meredith, an executive in the sales and technology space. Kathleen (1948-2003) predeceased him.

Robert remarried in 2009 to Gloria Lucy Balanta Rivera of Cali, Colombia, who joined him in Tiburon, where she currently resides.

In 1977, Robert joined Columbia Steel Casting Company, Inc., of Portland, Oregon, as district manager for the western states region. Over his 32-year career with the company, he became known for his innovative work in new product development and sales to the cement and waste-to-energy industries.

Outside of his career, Robert had a lifelong love of sports. He played football, baseball, tennis and boxed as a youth. He had a flair for salsa dancing and loved jazz and swing music. He also had a sincere commitment to serving others through Rotary International and the Sons in Retirement organization. item.title: Pick of the Week: Michael Jackson tribute Foreverland Sunday in Belvedere
item.description: Michael Jackson tribute band Foreverland closes this year’s Belvedere Concerts in the Park series at 4 p.m. Sept. 6 at the gazebo in Community Park.
item.content:encoded: Michael Jackson tribute band Foreverland closes this year’s Belvedere Concerts in the Park series at 4 p.m. Sept. 6 at the gazebo in Community Park. The 12-piece band uses no impersonator, playing instead as a celebration of the music — from The Jackson 5’s “I Want You Back” in the late ’60s through the disco of “Off the Wall” to the dance grooves of “Thriller” and beyond. The band, which has been playing events since 2009, builds its shows around the energy of the songs rather than the man who sang them. It is the fourth and last concert of the summer. Audiences picnic and dance on the lawn. The event is free.belvedereconcerts.org.

item.title: Four artists bring their ICB work to Tiburon Town Hall gallery
item.description: Work by four artists with studios in Sausalito's Industrial Center Building hangs in the Community Room at Tiburon Town Hall through Oct. 29.
item.content:encoded:
Kate Solari Baker has lived in Belvedere for 65 years and has kept the same studio in Sausalito for 47 of them. She has never hung a painting in Tiburon Town Hall.

That changes this month. Baker, 86, is one of four artists with studios in Sausalito’s Industrial Center Building whose work goes up in the upstairs Community Room at Town Hall through Oct. 29. The exhibit is titled “Nature, Reimagined: A Group Show by Artists from ICB Art,” and a reception is set for 6-8 p.m. Sept. 15.

item.media:description: Clockwise from top, screen print ‘Dolly’ by Bree Cutts, pastel ‘Marin Grasses’ by Kate Solari Baker, acrylic ‘Bright’ by Marine Strage and oil painting ‘New Heights’ by Lorrie Meyercord are among the works on display in ‘Nature, Reimagined: A Group Show by Artists from ICB Art’ at Tiburon Town Hall.

item.title: Federal prosecutors charge Tiburon man in $103M Pacific Private collapse
item.description: Mark Hanf of Tiburon, founder and former CEO of Novato-based Pacific Private Money, has been charged with charged in federal court with money laundering and conspiracy to commit wire fraud.
item.content:encoded:
A Tiburon man whose Novato lending firm took in about $103 million from investors before collapsing now faces federal fraud charges and has settled a case brought by securities regulators.

The charges against Mark Hanf come six months after The Ark reported that the Marin County District Attorney’s Office was fielding complaints from investors who could not get their money out.

Hanf, 66, the founder and former chief executive of Pacific Private Money, appeared in federal court in San Francisco on Sept. 1 and pleaded not guilty. So did Hoai-Nam Chu Phan, 58, of Novato, the former chief operating officer of Pacific Private Money Inc., the group’s operating company. Both are charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Hanf also faces a count of engaging in monetary transactions in criminally derived property, a money-laundering charge.

They settled the civil case the same day it was filed, each signing a consent to a judgment that would bar him permanently from the securities business. What they will owe has not been set.

The criminal charging document traces the collapse to a single death. Pacific Private Money raised investor capital to make loans secured by real property, paying members fixed distributions of about 6% to 10% a year and telling them they could take their principal back within 30 days without penalty. In 2021, prosecutors say, the developer who owed the most on loans from the firm’s original fund died. The document identifies him only as Developer-1. His loans were not being repaid, and the projects securing them were distressed and unlikely to cover what was owed.

That gutted the fund’s finances, prosecutors say, and Hanf and Phan did not tell investors the extent of the losses. By December 2021 the fund could not cover its expenses, its distributions and its redemptions out of revenue. On Dec. 7, 2021, the two began moving money between the Pacific Private funds to close the gap, booking the transfers as loans that accrued interest while little or no interest was actually paid. Money raised for one fund went out as distributions and redemptions to investors in another. Prosecutors put the total raised at about $103 million from more than 175 investors between December 2021 and December 2025.

“As alleged, these defendants falsely assured investors that Pacific Private Money was successful and profitable, knowing that continued losses had turned it into a Ponzi scheme,” U.S. Attorney Craig H. Mi...

item.title: Strawberry launches fundraising for its new playground
item.description: The Strawberry Recreation District has begun asking residents to help pay for its new playground under a program that would run from a $1,500 tile in aThe Strawberry Recreation District has begun asking residents to help pay for its new playground under a program that would run from a $1,500 tile in a mosaic to naming rights over the playground itself. mosaic to naming rights over the playground itself.
item.content:encoded:
The Strawberry Recreation District has begun asking residents to help pay for its new playground under a recognition schedule that would run from a $1,500 tile in a mosaic to naming rights over the playground itself.

The board approved a $2.4 million contract in July with playground company GameTime for a 12,799-square-foot play area off Belvedere Drive, centered on a climbable 20-foot-tall berry with two green slides for arms and bouncy footbridges. The district plans to break ground in 2027.

As drafted, donors who give less than $1,500 would be recognized on the district’s website. Above that the schedule offers permanent inscriptions on a bench, a picnic table, the park entry sign or a mosaic a local artist would make, rising to exclusive naming rights over the turf soccer field at $250,000 and over the playground at $500,000. Three levels are capped: 100 mosaic tiles, 10 benches and 10 picnic tables.

item.title: ‘Living shoreline’ restoration at Blackie’s starts after Labor Day
item.description: Work to rebuild two eroding beaches at Blackie's Pasture in Tiburon begins the day after Labor Day, using sand, gravel and logs instead of seawalls and riprap.
item.content:encoded:
Work to rebuild two eroding beaches at Blackie’s Pasture is set to begin the day after Labor Day, using sand, gravel and logs instead of seawalls and riprap to hold the shoreline in place.

The Tiburon Town Council voted 3-0 Aug. 19 to award the construction contract to Livermore-based Goodfellow Bros. for $468,983 and to let the town manager approve change orders of up to 15%, or $70,347, bringing the maximum to $539,330.

Goodfellow will grade back the eroding scarp, the steep face where the beach has been cut away. Crews will also remove and dispose of asphalt, install two rock sills at Brunini Beach and place a log backstop at Greenwood Beach.

“We’re installing a living shoreline, meaning that the material that’s being installed here at this beach, the wave action will pull the material out and push it back in so that it doesn’t erode any of the areas along Blackie’s Pasture,” said David Eshoo, the town Public Works Department’s engineering manager.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez
item.media:description: A project drawing shows the two beaches at Blackie’s Pasture as they would be rebuilt, with the beachface and backshore beach in tan, cobble-armored salt marsh and drift sills in green and the edges where vegetation is expected to take hold. The Tiburon Town Council awarded a $468,983 construction contract Aug. 19 to rebuild about 1.4 acres of shoreline along Greenwood and Brunini beaches with sand, gravel and logs instead of seawalls and riprap, and work is set to begin Sept. 8. (via town of Tiburon)

item.title: Tiburon will clear Railroad Marsh ahead of strong El Niño
item.description: Tiburon will strip about 1,800 tons of cattail, invasive plants and sediment from Railroad Marsh this fall to restore the basin's capacity to hold storm runoff.
item.content:encoded:
Crews will strip about 1,800 tons of cattail, invasive plants and sediment from Railroad Marsh this fall, restoring the basin’s capacity to hold storm runoff ahead of a winter federal forecasters put at better than a 90% chance of a very strong El Niño.

The Tiburon Town Council voted 4-0 Aug. 19 to hire Lafayette-based McNabb Construction Inc. for the work at a cost not to exceed $274,743 and to let the town manager approve change orders of up to 10%, bringing the ceiling to $302,217. Vice Mayor Isaac Nikfar was absent.

The contract sends the firm back to the marsh, where it did the town’s maintenance work last fall. McNabb was not the low bidder. Petaluma-based Land Revision bid $264,600, about $10,000 less, and Dixon Marine Services bid $386,237.

Public Works Engineering Manager David Eshoo told the council that staff will try to negotiate McNabb down to Land Revision’s price and that he does not expect to spend the contingency.

item.title: Tiburon monthly financial reports begin as audits lag
item.description: Tiburon's Town Council got its first monthly financial report Aug. 19, following months of resident pressure for more transparency about the town's books.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon’s Town Council received its first monthly financial report Aug. 19, a package that summed up the fiscal year that ended June 30, tallied the town’s cash and investments through July and laid out a decade of revenue and spending. Town Manager Greg Chanis cautioned that the year-end numbers are preliminary.

The presentation followed months of pressure from residents for more financial transparency, including calls to speed up the town’s audits and to create an independent finance committee like Belvedere’s.

Earlier in the meeting, on a separate item, Chanis addressed a question that has run through the criticism. Letters to the council had flagged revenue from hotel taxes, known as the transient occupancy tax, as coming in light for the year — the reports show the town’s two hotels generating $604,458 against $875,000 budgeted, a gap of $270,542. Chanis said that gap is an artifact of timing, not a shortfall. The tax arrives quarterly, in large chunks, and the final quarter ran six weeks late.

“Long story short, it looks like we’re going to exceed the budgeted revenue by several thousand dollars in (transient occupancy taxes),” Chanis said. “So the concern about a dramatic drop in (the tax) is not reality.”
